title: The first transatlantic phone cable carried 36 calls at once
body: The TAT-1 cable system entered service in 1956 with 36 telephone circuits across the Atlantic. A submerged cable could support conversations that did not rely on shortwave radio between continents.
takeaway: A route with a few dozen circuits changed what a long-distance conversation could sound like.
source: Bell System Technical Journal, Transatlantic Telephone Cable System (1958)

title: Whirlwind stored its working memory in tiny magnetic rings
body: In 1953 the MIT Whirlwind computer acquired its first working bank of magnetic core memory, with space for 2,048 words of data. Each small ring retained a bit through the direction of its magnetisation.
takeaway: A computer could keep its working bits in physical states that persisted without constant power.
source: Computer History Museum, Whirlwind Computer Debuts Core Memory (1953)
visual: a close view of a grid of tiny dark magnetic rings threaded with copper wires

title: A Norwegian simulation language helped introduce software objects
body: In the 1960s Kristen Nygaard and Ole-Johan Dahl created Simula to describe systems in which individual things interact. Simula helped pioneer object-oriented programming, where a model can group an entity's data with the operations it performs.
takeaway: A tool designed to model real systems ended up changing how people organised software generally.
source: Computer History Museum, First Reference to Simula in Writing
visual: a vintage computer console beside a small physical model of a factory

title: Standard ASCII fits its entire alphabet into seven bits
body: Developed in the 1960s, ASCII assigns a different pattern of seven bits to each of 128 entries. The entries include English letters, digits, punctuation and control signals such as a line break.
takeaway: Sharing a table like this let machines from different makers agree on the meaning of the same bits.
source: Computer History Museum, Internet History of the 1960s
